name: Discerning Solitary Salticid
subject: Biology
headline: A tiny spider may remember who it has met.
hook: A tiny loner spider may remember who it has met.
found: Jumping spiders told a familiar spider from a stranger.
matters: Big social smarts can fit in a very small brain.

drawing.subject: a cute regal jumping spider (Phidippus regius), drawn so it is clearly this species: a fuzzy jet-black body, a bold bright-white band across the front of its round abdomen with two white spots and white chevron stripes behind it, shiny iridescent metallic green-and-teal fangs (chelicerae) under its face, two huge glossy forward-facing main eyes with two smaller eyes beside them and more small eyes on top of its head, short sturdy legs ringed with white bands and tufts of white hair, and a little fringe of hair over its eyes like eyebrows. It is pressing its front legs against a clear plastic panel and looking through it, with a gentle look of recognition, at a second, smaller regal jumping spider on the other side of the panel, slightly out of focus
drawing.scene: Background: a simple lab test arena seen from just above, two small compartments separated by the clear panel, with soft warm lamp light and a blurred video camera overhead.

paper.hook:
Recognizing a familiar individual sounds like a big-brain skill. It helps animals find mates, avoid rivals and look after their young, and scientists usually link it to social species with large brains.

Jumping spiders don’t fit that picture. They are tiny hunters with excellent eyesight, but they mostly live alone and rarely meet the same spider twice. Earlier studies showed they can tell species and sex apart by colors and patterns. Nobody knew whether one could recognize a particular spider.
paper.found:
Dahl and Cheng set up face-to-face meetings between regal jumping spiders (Phidippus regius), kept safely apart by clear panels. A camera overhead tracked how close each pair chose to sit. Moving closer meant interest; keeping a distance meant less interest, or growing familiarity.

On a first meeting, a spider usually moved closer. When the same pair met again minutes later, they kept a little more distance. When the next meeting was with a different spider, they moved closer again. That switch between “seen you” and “someone new” repeated reliably across many pairings.

Interest faded as the same spiders were shown again, even hours later. Then, at the very end, a brand-new spider drew the strongest interest of all. A tired spider would lose interest in everything, so this late rebound suggests the spiders remembered who they had already seen and compared each new face with that memory.
paper.matters:
We often treat brain size as a shortcut for how clever an animal is. If a tiny, mostly solitary spider can keep track of individuals, flexible social memory may need far less brain than we assumed, and animals with small nervous systems may be underrated.

The same simple test can now be used on many other animals, to ask whether recognizing individuals follows an animal’s lifestyle and senses more than its brain size, and whether the skill evolved many separate times.

cite: Dahl, Christoph D., and Yaling Cheng. “Individual Recognition in a Jumping Spider (*Phidippus regius*).” *eLife*, vol. 13, 2025, article RP97146, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.97146.

name: Babbling Sac-winged Pup
subject: Biology
headline: Baby bats may benefit from more than a song playlist.
hook: Baby bats babble, just like human babies.
found: Pups with more involved mothers practiced longer and sounded more grown-up.
matters: Learning to talk may lean on caring parents in many animals.

drawing.subject: a cute baby bat pup hanging upside down from a branch, mouth open mid-babble, with two or three small curved sound lines coming from its mouth
drawing.scene: Background: the inside of a cave roost at dusk with its mother and other bats hanging in soft shadow behind.

paper.hook:
Human babies learn to talk by copying the sounds around them, and they get a lot of help along the way: smiles, gestures and encouragement from the people who care for them. Very few other animals learn their calls by imitating adults, and in those that do, little is known about how that kind of social feedback shapes learning.

Greater sac-winged bats, from the rainforests of Central and South America, are one of those rare learners. Their pups babble, a lot: nearly a third of their daytime activity goes to vocalizing and practicing the songs they hear from adult males. But the bats they spend the most time with are their mothers.
paper.found:
Fernandez and colleagues followed 19 pups in wild colonies in Panama and Costa Rica over two breeding seasons. They measured how long each pup practiced babbling, how many different song syllables it produced, and how much those syllables sounded like an adult male’s. They also tracked how often each mother interacted with her pup, for example by hovering over it or touching it, and how many singing males were nearby.

Pups with more involved mothers babbled longer each day and on more days overall. They also produced a wider variety of adult-like sounds, and more of their syllables sounded like a grown-up singer’s. Having more singing males nearby did not improve any of these measures.
paper.matters:
Most studies of vocal learning in animals pair one tutor with one learner in captivity. Watching wild bats shows that a youngster’s whole social world matters, not only the song it hears. Think of learning an instrument: hearing the tune and having company while you practice are two different parts of the experience.

Understanding how social feedback shapes song in other animals helps scientists piece together how vocal learning, and perhaps language, evolved.

cite: Fernandez, Ahana Aurora, et al. “Maternal Behavior Influences Vocal Practice and Learning Processes in the Greater Sac-Winged Bat.” *eLife*, vol. 13, 2025, article RP99474, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.99474.

name: Facilitative Weed-clipping Pika
subject: Biology
headline: A yak’s best friend might be a tiny gardener.
hook: Pika, called pests, may be a yak’s best friend.
found: Yaks gained more weight where some pika lived, because pika clip a poisonous plant.
matters: Wiping out a “pest” can backfire on the animals we care about.

drawing.subject: a cute pika (a small round-eared mountain mammal, like a tiny tailless rabbit) holding a clipped sprig of a poisonous purple-flowered plant in its mouth
drawing.scene: Background: a high grassy alpine meadow of the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau with rocks, short grass and a yak grazing far away.

paper.hook:
On the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, yaks share alpine meadows with the plateau pika, a small round-eared mammal. People disagree about pikas. Some call them serious pests that compete with yaks for food and damage pastures. Others call them a keystone species that keeps the ecosystem healthy and feeds many predators. Until this study, nobody had tested which view was right.

There was a clue. Pikas often clip, but don’t eat, a tall poisonous weed called Stellera. Under heavy grazing, Stellera has spread widely, crowding out the grasses and sedges that yaks need to eat.
paper.found:
Zhong and colleagues ran field experiments in which different patches of meadow had different numbers of pikas. The pikas cut down the tall Stellera, halving its cover. Freed from the weed, grasses and sedges grew more abundant, with 14% more crude protein, and yaks foraged 30–40% more efficiently.

The result: yaks gained up to 42% more weight per day where pikas were present. But only up to a point. The benefit peaked at about 200 pika burrows per hectare and turned negative above about 400, where the pikas became competitors for the same food.
paper.matters:
Wiping out every pika could backfire. Herders and rangeland managers could switch from killing pikas everywhere to keeping them at moderate numbers, below about 400 burrows per hectare, to help yaks grow while preventing outbreaks.

It is also a reminder that an animal’s role can depend on how many of them there are. The researchers say more work is needed at higher elevations, in winter, and with other livestock such as sheep.

cite: Zhong, Zhiwei, et al. “Small Mammalian Herbivores at Moderate Densities Facilitate Livestock Growth by Improving Vegetation Composition in Grasslands.” *eLife*, vol. 15, 2026, article RP111340, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.111340.

name: Synesthetic Pupillary Seven
subject: Psychology
headline: A gray number can make an eye react to color.
hook: For some people, a gray number looks colored.
found: Their pupils reacted to the color they experienced, though the screen stayed gray.
matters: The colors are real enough that the body responds to them.

drawing.subject: a cute gray number 7 character that glows warm orange around its edges, showing how a person with synesthesia sees a color in a gray number, with one big round curious eye beside it whose pupil is wide
drawing.scene: Background: a calm lab table with a computer screen showing gray numbers, like a perception experiment.

paper.hook:
What we see is not a straight copy of the world. It is built from the light that reaches the eye plus what the brain adds. In synesthesia, the brain’s addition is easy to spot: ordinary things trigger extra sensations. Someone might always see the number 5 as red, or hear a trumpet as bright yellow. It isn’t imagination or a choice; it simply happens.

The most common kind is grapheme–color synesthesia, where letters and numbers reliably come with colors. Most people who have it enjoy it, and the colors can even help them remember phone numbers. But because researchers have mostly had to rely on people’s own descriptions, it has been hard to measure.
paper.found:
Strauch, Leenaars and Rouw measured pupil size in 16 people with grapheme–color synesthesia and in two comparison groups of 16 people each, while everyone looked at gray digits on a screen.

The synesthetes’ pupils got smaller for digits that evoked brighter colors and larger for digits that evoked darker ones, even though every digit on the screen was the same gray. The responses were stronger for digits with a strong color link, and they came too quickly to be deliberate imagining.

The comparison group, asked to name a random color for each digit, showed no brightness effect. Their pupils also widened more, a sign that the task took them more effort than it took the synesthetes.
paper.matters:
The pupil works a bit like a camera’s aperture that responds partly to the brain’s version of the scene. Measuring it gives researchers a cheap, objective way to spot synesthesia and map how it varies, which helps show that these experiences are real. That matters for children with synesthesia, who are often misunderstood at school when they describe colored letters and numbers.

Because the color has no physical source on the screen, the method also helps scientists study how the brain builds what we consciously see.

cite: Strauch, Christoph, et al. “Pupil Size Reveals the Perceptual Quality and Effortless Nature of Synesthesia.” *eLife*, vol. 15, 2026, article RP110390, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.110390.

name: Statistical Neonatal Listener
subject: Psychology
headline: A newborn’s brain is already listening for the pattern.
hook: Babies just days old already notice sound patterns.
found: Their brains tracked repeats in syllables and in voices, even when the other kept changing.
matters: We may be born with a pattern finder that helps us learn to talk.

drawing.subject: a cute sleeping newborn baby wearing a soft blue EEG cap with small round electrodes, with gentle sound waves reaching its ear
drawing.scene: Background: a cozy hospital nursery with a crib and a soft monitor showing brain-wave lines.

paper.hook:
Imagine listening to a language you don’t know. Where does one word end and the next begin? Babies face this puzzle from birth, and yet they work out their mother tongue without anyone explaining it. By six months they recognize some common nouns, and by one year they say their first words.

One thing that helps is statistical learning: noticing which syllables tend to follow which. In English, many syllables can follow “the”, but “brocco” is almost always followed by “li”. What nobody knew was whether this pattern-spotting works only on syllables, or on any feature of a sound.
paper.found:
Fló and colleagues recorded the brain’s electrical activity in newborns up to four days old while they listened to specially built streams of speech. In one experiment the pattern was in the syllables, while the voice kept changing. In the other, the pattern was in the voices, while the syllables kept changing. Voice patterns inside a word never happen in real speech, so spotting them would not help with learning words.

The newborns’ brains picked up both kinds of pattern equally well. Afterwards, the babies heard made-up “pseudo-words”. A specific brain response appeared only for pseudo-words built from the syllable patterns, not from the voice patterns.
paper.matters:
Statistical learning looks like a general-purpose pattern finder that works on many features of sound, not only syllables. Yet from birth, the brain seems to treat only syllable patterns as possible words and to handle them with a dedicated network.

Together this suggests that babies arrive with a broad ability to detect patterns, which may play a bigger part in early language learning than scientists had thought.

cite: Fló, Ana, et al. “Statistical Learning beyond Words in Human Neonates.” *eLife*, vol. 13, 2025, article RP101802, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.101802.

name: Synurbic Allometric Sunflower
subject: Environment
headline: Being big helps some species live in cities, but not all.
hook: Most wild species avoid cities, but a few move right in.
found: Bigger plants coped better in cities; animals followed no one rule.
matters: There is no single recipe for living in a city.

drawing.subject: a tall, cheerful common sunflower (Helianthus annuus) drawn as a living creature: a big round face of brown seeds ringed by bright yellow petals, with two big friendly cartoon eyes and a small smile in the seed disc, broad green leaves held out like arms, growing tall and confident out of a crack in a city sidewalk and looking down kindly at a tiny shiny green ground beetle with big eyes beside its stem
drawing.scene: Background: a sunny city street corner with red-brick apartment buildings, a lamppost and a parked bicycle, painted in warm tones.

paper.hook:
Cities are usually bad news for wildlife. Many plants and animals disappear as towns grow, yet a few species seem to love city life. Scientists have spent decades asking what sets the winners apart.

One popular idea is body size. Size shapes how far a living thing can travel, what it eats and how it copes with change: a big bird can fly in and out of a city easily, while a small beetle may be stuck there. But earlier studies looked at only a few groups or a handful of cities, so nobody knew whether size mattered everywhere.
paper.found:
Callaghan and colleagues checked more than 30,000 plant and animal species from around the world, using recorded sightings to score how strongly each one is drawn to cities.

Most species avoided cities; only a small number thrived in them. Size did matter, but not in the same way for everyone. Bigger plants were generally more likely to cope with city life. In animals the pattern was all over the place: some groups showed the opposite trend, and many showed no link with size at all.
paper.matters:
There is no single recipe for city success. Size helps explain which species live in cities in some groups, but it is only one piece of the puzzle, alongside food, movement and habitat.

As cities keep spreading, knowing which species can live in them matters more and more. The team shared city scores for every species and an interactive tool for exploring the results, from moths and birds to orchids, so others can test new ideas.

cite: Callaghan, Corey T., et al. “Global Relationships between Body Size and Urban Affinity across More than 30,000 Plant and Animal Species.” *eLife*, vol. 14, 2026, article RP109047, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.109047.

name: Heterodont Bathyal Sixgill
subject: Biology
headline: A shark’s whole set of teeth tells where it lives.
hook: One shark tooth is a clue; a whole mouthful tells a story.
found: How neighboring teeth differ matched where a shark lives.
matters: Fossil teeth may show how ancient oceans changed.

drawing.subject: a friendly bluntnose sixgill shark (Hexanchus griseus), drawn so it is clearly this species: a long, dark brownish-gray body, six gill slits on each side of its head, a single small dorsal fin set far back near the tail, a blunt rounded snout and big glowing green eyes, with a shy, gentle open-mouthed grin that shows its two kinds of teeth: wide comb-shaped teeth with many little points along the lower jaw and narrower hooked teeth in the upper jaw
drawing.scene: Background: the dim blue deep sea just above a muddy seafloor, with soft light fading down from above into darkness.

paper.hook:
Teeth come in a huge variety of shapes, fitted to every kind of diet and home. They differ between species, between animals of the same species, and even within one mouth, which often holds several kinds of teeth.

Sharks and mammals both have especially varied teeth, though their last common ancestor lived hundreds of millions of years ago. A tooth is built in layers of detail: where it sits in the jaw is settled first, then its small points (cusps) and saw edges. Single shark teeth had been studied before, but not how a whole set of teeth fits a shark’s way of life.
paper.found:
Zimm and colleagues built a new way to compare entire sets of teeth, using an online collection of shark teeth together with genetic data on how the species are related.

They found clear differences between the two major groups of sharks and between the places sharks live, especially the deep sea and the open ocean. How neighboring teeth in the same jaw differ from one another was shaped more by a shark’s home than by its family tree. Ancestry explained more of the fine details within each tooth and the differences between the upper and lower jaws.
paper.matters:
Many body parts work as a team across scales, from a tiny saw edge to a whole jaw. This study shows which level of detail tells you about a lifestyle and which tells you about ancestry.

Shark teeth often survive as fossils, and they are closely tied to how a shark feeds and where it lives. Reading whole sets of teeth could help scientists follow how ocean life changed in the past and predict how it may change next.

cite: Zimm, Roland, et al. “Integration of Multi-Level Dental Diversity Links Macro-Evolutionary Patterns to Ecological Strategies across Sharks.” *eLife*, vol. 14, 2025, article e107406, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.107406.

name: Sequestering Polytoxic Monarch
subject: Chemistry
headline: Even a poison expert struggles with a toxic cocktail.
hook: Monarch caterpillars eat poisonous milkweed and keep the poison.
found: A mix of five poisons slowed them more than any single one.
matters: A mix of defenses can wear down a specialist pest.

drawing.subject: a plump, cute monarch butterfly caterpillar (Danaus plexippus), drawn so it is clearly this species: bold bands of black, white and yellow around its body, a pair of black whip-like filaments at the front and a shorter pair at the back, small black legs, and big cartoon eyes on its round face, chewing a tropical milkweed leaf (Asclepias curassavica) with a slightly overwhelmed, puffed-cheek look, beside a small cluster of the plant's red-and-orange flowers
drawing.scene: Background: a sunny lab bench with small round milkweed leaf discs in clear petri dishes, in warm lamp light.

paper.hook:
Monarch butterflies eat only milkweed, a plant loaded with poisons called cardenolides. Monarchs have evolved not just to survive these poisons but to store them in their bodies, which protects them from predators such as birds. It is a textbook arms race between a plant and the insect that eats it.

But plants rarely make just one poison. Some milkweeds also make unusual cardenolides that contain nitrogen and sulfur, and nobody knew whether these, or the mixture as a whole, cost monarch caterpillars more than the familiar ones.
paper.found:
Agrawal and colleagues purified the five main cardenolides from tropical milkweed (Asclepias curassavica) and fed them to monarch caterpillars, one at a time or all mixed together.

The caterpillars did not store the nitrogen- and sulfur-containing poisons as they were. They changed them into less toxic forms first, so they ended up with less defensive poison than caterpillars fed the other toxins.

The mixture hit hardest. Caterpillars fed all five toxins together grew more slowly and stored less poison than those fed the same amount of single compounds. The variety itself seems to overwhelm the caterpillar’s detox system.
paper.matters:
A plant’s defense is more than its strongest poison: a mix of chemicals can wear down even a specialist that has evolved to eat it.

Farmers could borrow this cocktail approach, protecting crops with several compounds at once instead of relying on one. The next step is to test the idea on living plants and with many other plant-eating insects.

cite: Agrawal, Anurag A., et al. “Cardenolide Toxin Diversity Impacts Monarch Butterfly Growth and Sequestration.” *eLife*, vol. 14, 2026, article RP109003, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.109003.

name: Resilient Riparian Burrower
subject: Earth science
headline: Life rebuilt a busy riverbank soon after Earth’s worst extinction.
hook: Earth’s worst extinction wiped out most life 252 million years ago.
found: Two million years later, a riverbank near the equator was busy again.
matters: Burrowing may help life ride out extreme heat.

drawing.subject: a cute ancient freshwater crayfish with big cartoon eyes on short stalks, a reddish-brown segmented shell, two sturdy claws and long antennae, peeking proudly out of the round entrance of its burrow in a muddy riverbank, the burrow winding down between pale plant roots
drawing.scene: Background: an Early Triassic riverbank 250 million years ago under a hot, hazy sky, with tall jointed horsetail-like Neocalamites stems and Pleuromeia plants (single upright stems topped with a tuft of grassy leaves) along a shallow muddy river, and far in the distance a small lizard-like reptile with a long tail.

paper.hook:
About 252 million years ago, Earth suffered its worst mass extinction. Huge volcanic eruptions, global warming and acid rain wiped out more than 95% of ocean species and about 70% of life on land, and the planet stayed harsh for millions of years.

Some sea life seems to have bounced back fairly quickly, but recovery on land is much harder to study, because few fossils survive, especially from basins near the equator. So how fast did land ecosystems there come back?
paper.found:
Guo and colleagues studied rock layers from the very end of the Permian and the start of the Triassic at six sites in the Central North China Basin, which lay near the equator at the time.

They found new fossils of medium-sized meat-eating reptiles, plant stems, root traces and many burrows, including crayfish burrows tangled in plant roots. Animals were living down in the riverbank mud far more than before.

Together these clues point to a river-side ecosystem with several levels of eaters, from burrowers to predators, about two million years after the extinction. Land life near the equator may have recovered faster and more fully than scientists assumed.
paper.matters:
The study helps explain how Earth became livable again after the disaster. It suggests that around 250 million years ago, plants and animals adapted fairly quickly to extreme heat, for example by burrowing underground and living along rivers.

That makes these ancient riverbanks a guide to how living things might respond to severe global warming in the future.

cite: Guo, Wenwei, et al. “Rapid Riparian Ecosystem Recovery in Low-Latitudinal North China following the End-Permian Mass Extinction.” *eLife*, vol. 14, 2026, article RP104205, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.104205.

name: Latent Ocellar Formicine
subject: Genetics
headline: Evolution may keep an old blueprint in the drawer.
hook: Worker ants lost their tiny extra eyes, then kept getting them back.
found: Eye-building genes still flicker on in workers with no extra eyes.
matters: A lost trait’s recipe can hide, ready to return.

drawing.subject: a cute worker formicine ant drawn so it is clearly an ant: a reddish-brown body in three parts (head, thorax and a round, shiny abdomen), bent elbowed antennae, six thin legs, two big glossy compound eyes as its cartoon eyes, and three tiny glowing simple eyes (ocelli) arranged in a little triangle on top of its head, which it is trying to look up at with a curious, delighted expression
drawing.scene: Background: inside an underground ant nest, warm earthen tunnels and chambers, with a few pale white larvae resting in a soft-lit chamber.

paper.hook:
Sometimes a body part disappears during evolution and then comes back millions of years later. How a lost trait can return is an old puzzle.

Ants are a good place to look. In one colony the same genes can build queens, males and workers that look very different. Queens and males always have ocelli, three tiny light-sensing eyes on top of the head. Workers have lost and regained them again and again: depending on the species, a worker has none, one, two or all three.
paper.found:
Vasquez-Correa and colleagues traced the family history of worker ocelli across a huge group of ants, the Formicinae. Workers gained ocelli once, then lost them many times and got them back independently several times.

To see how, they watched the head develop from the eye-antennal disc, the tissue that builds the eyes, antennae, ocelli and head. A staining method lit up genes as they switched on. Even in workers with no ocelli, key ocellus-building genes were briefly active: the genetic recipe was still there, just never finished.
paper.matters:
When a trait is lost, its instructions may not be. A dormant recipe like this could explain how ocelli kept coming back in worker ants and soldiers.

Many living things grow different forms from the same genes, from single cells to whole societies. If hidden gene activity like this is common, it could be a store of evolutionary potential that helps lost traits return in new forms.

cite: Vasquez-Correa, Angelly, et al. “Latent Gene Network Expression Underlies Partial Re-Evolution of a Polyphenic Trait in the Worker Caste of Ants.” *eLife*, vol. 15, 2026, article RP110148, https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.110148.
